name: Jere
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2020. The East Kainji languages of Central Nigeria. Afrika und Übersee 93: 45-92. DOI 10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.210 (open access).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 Phonology (pp. 54-58) uses eBoze as the worked example; 'Tones' p. 57: 'Boze has four level tones as well as rising and falling tones', superhigh from a plural tone-raising rule, glide tones. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the article. Jere/Zele proper appears only in the language table (p. 49, 'Vigorous', source Gowers 1907).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2021. Introduction to the Shammɔ peoples of Central Nigeria. Draft ms., Jos, 12 pp. (sec. 2.3 Zele [=Jere], p. 7).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ethnographic; states 'The only strictly linguistic publication on this language [Zele] is Shimizu (1980), a Swadesh list with grammatical notes' [= Shimizu 1982a]; a Reading and Writing Book prepared 2019 but unreleased; 'Speakers state that Zele is closest to Gusu.' Nothing on phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2019. Atlas of Nigerian Languages, ed. IV, entry 216 Jere cluster (Jere/Ezelle; Ibunu-Lɔrɔ; Boze; Panawa).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Bibliographic only: Refs Shimizu (1968, 1980, 1982); 'Grammar: Shimizu (1968)' for Ibunu; sources IL/NBTT wordlists. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. (with the Boze literacy committee). 2018 [printout 1 Jan 2019]. Dictionary of the ɛBoze language of Central Nigeria. Draft circulated for comment, 125 pp. (Glottolog ref 569157, 'Boze = Jere [jer]').
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3 Phonology (vowels, consonants, tones); sec. 3.3 Tones p. 5 (PDF p. 7): 'εBoze has three level tones and rising and falling tones. However, a superhigh tone occurs on some nouns with a tone-raising rule.' 'Normally, nouns exhibit only three levels within a word.' Nothing on stress/accent-as-prominence in the whole file (only 'acute accent' etc. as diacritic names).

sources.note: Sec. 3.5.2 ɛBoze: noun-class prefixes and their tone (singular prefix low, plural raised); no stress statement.
